meta.ced_version: AP CSP Course and Exam Description, effective Fall 2023 (V.1)
meta.section_ii_format: on-exam-day written response with Personalized Project Reference
meta.mcq_format: 70 multiple-choice questions in 120 minutes, worth 70% of the exam score: 57 individual single-select, 8 individual multi-select (65 individual questions total), plus one 5-question single-select set tied to a computing-innovation reading passage
meta.class_periods_note: The CED's 'Course at a Glance' table does not list a suggested number of class periods per topic. The numbers printed next to each topic in that table are references to Computational Thinking Practice numbers (1-6, see the practices list), not time estimates. Every topic below carries class_periods: null for this reason, not because extraction failed.
meta.practice_note: Practice 6 (Responsible Computing) is not assessed on the multiple-choice section at all -- it is assessed only through the Create Performance Task -- so it carries no MCQ weight range.

topics.title: Collaboration
topics.paraphrase: Working with other people, and giving them credit, changes how a computing project turns out.
topics.note: No pair-programming or collaborative-workflow content anywhere in the book. Taught continuously, through lab pair work and the Create Performance Task, not as a standalone lesson.

topics.title: Program Function and Purpose
topics.paraphrase: A program exists to do something for someone, and describing what it does means naming its inputs, its outputs, and the behavior that connects them.
topics.note: chap01 frames programs generally; chap05's 'Keyboard input' section is the book's only real input-handling content. The CED's event-driven-programming framing (CRD-2.C.5, CRD-2.C.6) has no counterpart -- this book's programs are run-to-completion scripts, not event loops.

topics.title: Program Design and Development
topics.paraphrase: Building a program well means planning before writing, documenting while writing, and being willing to revise.
topics.note: chap04's 'A development plan' and 'Docstrings' sections are a direct match for CRD-2.E/F/G. CRD-2.H (acknowledging code taken from another source) has no counterpart anywhere in the book -- a real gap, not just a light topic.

topics.title: Identifying and Correcting Errors
topics.paraphrase: Programs fail in a few recognizable ways, and testing with well-chosen inputs -- including edge cases -- is how those failures get found before a user does.
topics.note: Every chapter in the book carries a 'Debugging' section, confirmed by header scan. That is the strongest and most consistent alignment of any Big Idea 1 topic; chap07's doctest material additionally matches CRD-2.J's testing-with-defined-inputs framing well.

topics.title: Binary Numbers
topics.paraphrase: Computers store everything as bits, and binary place-value works the same way decimal place-value does, just base 2 instead of base 10.
exclusions: specific range limitations for real numbers are outside course/exam scope (EK DAT-1.B.3)
topics.note: Carried by the interlude between chapters 7 and 8 ('Representing Data', chap07b): bits, place value, binary/decimal/hex conversion by hand and via bin()/int(s, 2)/format(). As of 2026-08-17 chap07b exists only as an outline (section headings, vocabulary, standards claims) -- no drafted prose or exercises yet; see CHAPTER_MANIFEST.md's Interludes section and AUDIT.md's 2026-08-17 handoff. Previously logged as carried by CS50T Multimedia; that supplement was dropped after year one and never taught again, so the assignment was stale -- removed 2026-08-09 per teacher confirmation. The Pico/MicroPython unit's I2C chapter (source/rpi-pico-2e ch.14, 'Digital communication protocols') remains a secondary, partial touchpoint (hexadecimal as byte notation) alongside chap07b's fuller treatment.

topics.title: Data Compression
topics.paraphrase: Compression trades off file size against fidelity; lossless keeps everything, lossy throws some of it away for a bigger size reduction.
topics.note: Carried by the interlude between chapters 7 and 8 ('Representing Data', chap07b): the lossless/lossy contrast, taught as the choice the exam actually tests rather than as definitions, plus student-written run-length encoding as the lossless worked example. As of 2026-08-17 chap07b exists only as an outline -- no drafted prose or exercises yet; see CHAPTER_MANIFEST.md's Interludes section and AUDIT.md's 2026-08-17 handoff. Previously logged as carried by CS50T Multimedia; removed 2026-08-09 per teacher confirmation that supplement hasn't been taught since year one. The Pico I2C chapter (see 2.1's note) still doesn't touch compression at all.

topics.title: Extracting Information from Data
topics.paraphrase: Raw data becomes information once a program finds the patterns in it, and real data sets are rarely clean enough to do that without some processing first.
topics.note: chap12 (word frequencies, Markov analysis) and chap13 (file/database work) are a strong match. Metadata specifically (DAT-2.B) has no direct counterpart.

topics.title: Using Programs with Data
topics.paraphrase: Programs that read, combine, and rewrite data files let a person do with a data set what would be impractical by hand.
topics.note: chap13's file, YAML, and shelve work carries this directly.

topics.title: Variables and Assignments
topics.paraphrase: A variable is a named place to keep a value, and assignment is how that name gets pointed at a value.

topics.title: Data Abstraction
topics.paraphrase: Grouping related values under one name lets a program treat a collection as a single thing instead of tracking each part separately.
exclusions: linked lists are outside course/exam scope (EK AAP-1.D.6)
topics.note: Lists (chap09), dictionaries (chap10), and tuples (chap11) are all worked examples of this LO. The linked-list exclusion is moot here -- the book never implements one.

topics.title: Mathematical Expressions
topics.paraphrase: Arithmetic and comparison operators combine into expressions the same way in code as they do on paper, with the same rules about order of operations.

topics.title: Strings
topics.paraphrase: Text is data too, and a string is handled as a sequence of characters that can be measured, sliced, and searched.

topics.title: Boolean Expressions
topics.paraphrase: An expression that evaluates to true or false is what a program's decisions are built on.

topics.title: Conditionals
topics.paraphrase: An if-statement lets a program take one path or another depending on whether a condition holds.

topics.title: Nested Conditionals
topics.paraphrase: Putting one conditional inside another lets a program handle more than two possible outcomes.

topics.title: Iteration
topics.paraphrase: Repeating a block of statements, either a fixed number of times or until some condition changes, is how a program does the same kind of work over and over.
topics.note: IMPORTANT COVERAGE GAP, not a light-topic judgment call: the exam reference sheet gives this topic two pseudocode forms -- REPEAT n TIMES (definite, matches Python's `for`) and REPEAT UNTIL(condition) (indefinite/condition-controlled, matches Python's `while`). This edition of the book has no `while` loop anywhere -- confirmed by scanning every code cell in chapters 1-13, zero hits outside prose mentions of the English word 'while'. Indefinite iteration is instead handled through recursion (chap05, chap06), which is a real substitute conceptually but is not the same pseudocode construct on the exam, and does not produce the REPEAT UNTIL-specific edge cases the CED calls out (AAP-2.K.4 infinite loop from a condition that never becomes true; AAP-2.K.5 zero-iteration when the condition is already true) since Python's recursion has no direct exam-reference-sheet form of its own. Whether this is closed with a short while-loop supplement or left as recursion-covers-it-in-spirit is a real pedagogical call, not something to resolve while indexing the standard.

topics.title: Developing Algorithms
topics.paraphrase: Building an algorithm from scratch usually means starting with a rough version and refining it in small, testable steps.
topics.note: chap06's 'Incremental development' section is a direct match; chap07 builds a linear-search function the same way.

topics.title: Lists
topics.paraphrase: A list holds an ordered sequence of values that a program can step through one at a time.
exclusions: traversing two lists at once with a shared index (parallel traversal) is outside course/exam scope (EK AAP-2.O.1)

topics.title: Binary Search
topics.paraphrase: Searching a sorted collection by repeatedly cutting the remaining range in half finds a value in far fewer steps than checking every element.
exclusions: specific implementations of the binary search algorithm are outside course/exam scope (EK AAP-2.P.1)
topics.note: The book teaches linear search explicitly (chap07, named 'linear search' in the text) but never introduces binary search, even conceptually -- no `bisect`, no sorted-list halving example anywhere. Taught in the November algorithms block.

topics.title: Calling Procedures
topics.paraphrase: Calling a function hands control to a separate block of code and, often, gets a value back in return.

topics.title: Developing Procedures
topics.paraphrase: Writing a function well means giving it parameters general enough to be reused, and a name and docstring that explain what it does without exposing how.

topics.title: Libraries
topics.paraphrase: Importing a library brings in code someone else already wrote and tested, so a program can use it without reimplementing it.
topics.note: chap02 introduces `import`; chap04 (jupyturtle) and chap08 (`re`) are the book's main worked examples of using an imported library.

topics.title: Random Values
topics.paraphrase: A program can introduce controlled unpredictability by drawing values from a random-number generator instead of computing them.

topics.title: Simulations
topics.paraphrase: A simulation stands in for a real process that would be too slow, risky, or expensive to run for real, trading some realism for repeatability.
topics.note: No dedicated simulation content in chapters 1-13; 'simulation' as a word only surfaces in chap19 (independent-study range, not this topic's natural home). chap12's random-number work is adjacent but not the same idea (generating text, not modeling a process). Taught in the November algorithms block.

topics.title: Algorithmic Efficiency
topics.paraphrase: Algorithms that solve the same problem are not equally fast, and how an algorithm's running time grows with input size is what separates a practical solution from an impractical one.
exclusions: formal/mathematical (Big-O) analysis of algorithms is outside course/exam scope (EK AAP-4.A.3)
specific heuristic solutions are outside course/exam scope (EK AAP-4.A.9)
topics.note: No informal efficiency discussion (counting statement executions, comparing two algorithms for the same problem) appears anywhere in chapters 1-13. Occurrences of the word 'efficient' in the book are incidental, not this topic. Taught in the November algorithms block.

topics.title: Undecidable Problems
topics.paraphrase: Some yes-or-no problems have no algorithm that can always answer correctly, no matter how much time is allowed.
exclusions: determining whether a given problem is undecidable is outside course/exam scope (EK AAP-4.B.2)
topics.note: Not carried by this book at all; a conceptual, non-programming topic. Taught in the November algorithms block.

topics.title: The Internet
topics.paraphrase: The internet moves data between computers by breaking it into pieces and routing each piece independently through a shared network of devices.

topics.title: Fault Tolerance
topics.paraphrase: A system built from unreliable parts can still be reliable overall if it is designed to keep working when some of those parts fail.

topics.title: Parallel and Distributed Computing
topics.paraphrase: Splitting a problem across multiple processors or machines can finish it faster than one processor working alone.

topics.title: Beneficial and Harmful Effects
topics.paraphrase: A computing innovation can end up used in ways its creators never intended, for better and for worse.

topics.title: Digital Divide
topics.paraphrase: Unequal access to computing and the internet, across geography, income, and other lines, shapes who benefits from computing innovations.

topics.title: Computing Bias
topics.paraphrase: Software can reproduce and amplify existing human biases, whether through the data it learns from or the assumptions built into its logic.

topics.title: Crowdsourcing
topics.paraphrase: Gathering small contributions from very large numbers of people, over the internet, can solve problems no small group could tackle alone.

topics.title: Legal and Ethical Concerns
topics.paraphrase: Digitizing information raises questions of ownership and proper credit that copying on paper never had to answer at the same scale.

topics.title: Safe Computing
topics.paraphrase: Personal data collected online carries real risk, and encryption and authentication are the main tools for limiting who can get at it.
exclusions: specific mathematical procedures for encryption/decryption are outside course/exam scope (EK IOC-2.B.5)
